subLevels.reveal: Well done! Pay attention to these reveals — they may help with future puzzles, tell you a fun fact, or pose a bonus mini-puzzle! For example, the city of Salzburg in Austria is famous for its music 🎵 but what else is it famous for mining? You can already guess!

German likes its compound words, as we're going to find out! English is a bit more variable in whether it writes compounds as one word or two, with hyphens or without. German just gloms two words, three words, four and more together!

hints.hint: Meer and French "mer" have the same meaning.

subLevels.reveal: English still retains "mere" in some place names like "Windermere", the largest lake in England.

subLevels.reveal: Indeed, the excess salt in seawater would dehydrate you more than drinking nothing at all. Therefore, Meerwasser ist kein Trinkwasser.

subLevels.german: Wasser, Wasser überall, und nicht ein Tropfen zu trinken.

hints.hint: The lament of the Ancient Mariner

subLevels.reveal: Coleridge's ballad actually says "Nor any drop to drink", but who quotes it like that? No one.

subLevels.german: Ich trinke Bier, du trinkst Milch.
subLevels.reveal: Fun fact! German du ~ "thou" in English!

subLevels.english: I drink beer, you drink milk.
subLevels.explanation: German has two slots at the front of basic sentences that must be filled. By default, the first slot holds the subject, but other elements can be spotlighted by placing them here instead. The conjugated verb is the one thing that can't go here; it must always go in the second slot. An "invalid move" is any move that violates these rules.

hints.hint: To move a word, tap on it and then its destination, or drag (only on desktop). To return a yellow word (meaning it meets the rules, but isn't the word order we're looking for), tap on it again.

subLevels.reveal: This may not seem very exciting yet: it's exactly the same word order as in English. But we'll soon see how these rules add up to produce the logic of the infamous German word order!

subLevels.english: It's beer that I drink, it's milk that you drink.

hints.hint: We're looking for a different word order from the last puzzle. Tap on a yellow word to return it to its original position.

subLevels.reveal: By putting the objects into the first slot, we draw attention to their contrast. Note, though: the English translation is clunky and a lot stronger than the German. For example, if I ask "What are you drinking?" you could naturally respond with Bier trinke ich, putting the answer in the first slot. But if you responded in English with "It's beer that I drink", that would be really weird!

subLevels.german: Ich habe Kaffee, du hast Tee.

hints.hint: Since du is just old-timey "thou", hast is just old-timey...?

subLevels.reveal: Old English said "ic hæbbe" too, but English gradually smooshed together most present tense forms (except "has") while German kept alllll its verb distinctions.

hints.hint: This is our first sentence with a significant word order difference. Where one language has 1234, the other language has 1243.
Change the u of getrunken to an i to find a more familiar verb we've seen a few times already.
getrunken is the past participle of trinken. For example "taken" is the past participle of "take".

subLevels.reveal: This was objectively the hardest puzzle in this level! Well done! By the way, this German sentence is also the everyday way to say "I drank beer". Now let's see why the word order is the way it is!

We're starting to see the word order differences from English! Here, it's the auxiliary verb habe that has the tense and is conjugated to agree with the subject ich, hence it goes in that verb-second (V2) slot, leaving its past participle getrunken alone at the end of the sentence. Whereas in English, "have" and "drunk" would have stayed together.

subLevels.german: Ich habe zu viel Wein getrunken.
subLevels.reveal: We saw zu meaning "to" earlier, and as you can see here, it also means "too", whereas English spells them differently.

hints.hint: The obvious consequence of the previous sentence.
